title: Derivative, differentiability, tangent, and normal
terms: derivative; difference quotient; secant line; tangent line; normal line; differentiability; corner; cusp; vertical tangent; Leibniz notation.

Secant slopes use finite increments; differentiation takes their limit.
Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability. Corners
have unequal one-sided slopes; vertical tangents have unbounded slopes and do not give finite
derivatives. A derivative may exist without being continuous. Prime notation, df /dx, and the
operator d/dx describe the same first derivative. Piecewise differentiability requires matching
both values and one-sided difference quotients.

question.text:
2
Let f(0) = 0 and f(x) = x sin(1/x) for x ̸= 0. Which statement holds?
(A) f is discontinuous at zero.
(B) f is continuous but not differentiable at zero.
′ ′
(C) f (0) = 0, but f is not continuous at zero.
′
(D) f (0) = 1.
′
(E) f is continuous at zero.

solution.text:
′ ′
The difference quotient is x sin(1/x), which tends to zero, so f (0) = 0. For x ̸= 0, f (x) =
2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x), whose cosine term has distinct subsequential limits. Existence of a
derivative at a point does not make the derivative continuous there.

question.text:
3
The tangent to y = x at a positive point intersects the y-axis at −16. What is its slope?
(A) 8 (B) 6 (C) 16 (D) 24 (E) 12

solution.text:
2 3 3 2
At x = a, the tangent is y = 3a x − 2a . Thus a = 8, so a = 2 and the slope is 3a = 12.

question.text:
2
At which real points is |x − 1| not differentiable?
(A) x = −1, 0, 1 only (B) Nowhere (C) x = −1, 1 only (D) x = 0 only (E) x = 1 only

solution.text:
2
At the simple zeros ±1 of x − 1, taking absolute value reverses the sign of a nonzero slope,
producing corners. Away from these zeros the expression is locally a polynomial.
